title: Anatomy of an in-the-money debit call spread
summary: An in-the-money debit call spread is a positive-carry trade with a bullish tilt: if the underlying does nothing, time decay works for you. The example SPY 720/730 call spread costs $8 for a $10 width, makes 25% anywhere above $730 (about 3.3% lower; breakeven about 3.6% lower), and loses the full premium below the long strike.

steps.caption: SPY trades near $755. We buy the 720 call and sell the 730 call, one month out: both strikes are below the market.
The dashed lines are the two legs at expiry: a long call and a short call that caps the gain.
Together: pay about $8 for a $10 wide spread. Above $730 at expiry the spread is worth $10.
Maximum profit is the width minus the debit, about $2 per share: 25% on the premium.
Breakeven sits near $728, about 3.6% below the market. The full 25% needs SPY above $730, a fall of at most about 3.3%.
Positive carry: with SPY unchanged, the blue curve rises toward the maximum as expiry approaches. You are net long theta.
The risk: below $720 at expiry you lose 100% of the premium. Size for that full loss.
The 3D surface shows P&L across price and time: the profit plateau grows as the days pass.

takeaways: An ITM debit call spread has the same payoff as an OTM put credit spread at the same strikes.
It earns from time decay when the price stays put, so it fits mildly bullish or sideways markets.
The reward is small relative to the risk: a drop below the long strike loses the full debit, so size small.
caveats: Reward:risk is about 0.25:1. The owner's X09 rule needs logged hit-rate evidence before deploying it.
The speaker's 'still makes 25% after a 4.9% fall' does not fit 720/730 at $755: a 4.9% fall (~$718) is below the long strike, a full loss. 25% holds only above $730 (-3.3%).

backtest.note: One-month spread with both strikes in the money; exit at 20% gained on the debit (80% of the maximum) or 60% lost.
